doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: His high school dance band: repertoire and playing where beer was served
summary: The band played stock arrangements of hits; Fillius sang, and his parents once caught him at a beer place.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: I think it’s a good term. What was the repertoire that your particular dance band would play?
Oh gee. “Blue Moon,” “Red Sails in the Sunset,” we did a novelty thing called “Old Man Mose” and I was the singer.
Oh yeah. And we did “White Heat,” Jimmy Lunceford’s “White Heat.” We just bought standard, off the shelf arrangements. “Harbor Lights,” all the tunes of the times. The kids loved to dance to them.
So you played like high school dances?

Oh yeah. My father had laid down the rule that I could not go anyplace they served booze. And I pretty much obeyed that until one night I was at a place called the Dutch Mill in Rochester, which is near where my wife used to live and where I used to live. And they served beer. And we were in the bandstand playing away and I looked up and there my mother and father are dancing. So I caught hell for it. But I actually never had a drink. I never touched it until I came here to the college. All the way through high school and all the way through those days, I didn’t drink although I played in many places, really,
where they served drinks. They weren’t heavy hitters like they have now but there were places where they served beer. And most people don’t get too drunk on beer.
